passages.happening:
‘And Job continued his discourse’ (verse 1). “How I long for the months gone by, for the days when God watched over me, when His lamp shone above my head, and by His light I walked through the darkness” (verses 2-3).

He remembers ‘when the friendship of God rested on my tent, when the Almighty was still with me and my children were around me’ (verses 4-5), when his steps were bathed in cream and the rock poured out streams of oil for him.
passages.hearers:
This chapter opens Job's final speech, chapters 29 to 31, his closing statement before God. Its three parts move like a legal case: past honor (chapter 29), present shame (chapter 30), and an oath of innocence with a challenge to God to answer (chapter 31). The friends have fallen silent, and Job speaks to no one in particular.

The Hebrew behind ‘How I long’ (verse 2) is literally who will give, the idiom Job uses elsewhere for his deepest wishes.

The word for friendship in verse 4, sod, means the close circle where secrets are shared. It is a remarkably intimate picture of what Job once had with God. And notice the order of what he misses most: first God's friendship, then his children around him.

Cream and oil are poetic pictures of plenty, recalling the language of the promised land.
passages.asks: Job's memory of the good years began with God's friendship and his children around him. Ask what you remember most from a better season. And ask whether you can thank God for it without pretending the loss does not hurt.

passages.happening:
When Job went out to the city gate and took his seat, young men stepped back, old men stood up, princes stopped talking and covered their mouths, and nobles fell silent.

Why? ‘Because I rescued the poor who cried out and the fatherless who had no helper. The dying man blessed me, and I made the widow’s heart sing for joy’ (verses 12-13). “I put on righteousness, and it clothed me; justice was my robe and my turban. I served as eyes to the blind and as feet to the lame. I was a father to the needy, and I took up the case of the stranger” (verses 14-16). ‘I shattered the fangs of the unjust and snatched the prey from his teeth’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The city gate was the center of a town's public life. In ancient towns the gate complex had chambers and benches where elders sat, legal cases were heard, business was done and announcements were made. Archaeologists have uncovered such gates at a number of Iron Age sites in the land of Israel.

The ideal of a leader who defends the vulnerable was widespread. Kings across the ancient Near East claimed to protect widows and orphans, and Israel's law made the same care a religious duty (Exodus 22:22-24). Job describes himself as living out that ideal as a private citizen.

Clothing in that world signaled rank and office, and the turban was worn by people of standing. Job means that justice was not something he put on for show. It was the very identity by which he was known.

This chapter answers Eliphaz's charges in chapter 22 that Job oppressed widows, orphans and the poor. Job's memory paints the opposite picture, and the reader knows from the prologue that his memory is true.
passages.later: The Psalms give God the title Job had earned among his neighbors: “A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in His holy habitation” (Psalm 68:5).
passages.hard:
Is Job boasting? He describes his own righteousness and honor at length.

Some readers find the chapter uncomfortable. Job speaks of how others honored him, how princes fell silent before him and how he sat like a king, and it can sound like pride. Elihu and God will later challenge Job, and some interpreters think this chapter shows why: Job's sense of himself was bound up with his standing and his good works. Other readers point out that the chapter is a legal defense, not a boast. Eliphaz accused Job of oppressing the poor, and Job answers by describing what he actually did. The narrator and God himself confirm that Job was blameless and upright (1:1; 1:8).

Most interpreters see both. Job's account is true and his goodness was real, yet the chapter also shows how much his sense of himself depended on honor and on being needed. When that was taken, he lost more than possessions.
passages.asks: Job was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame. Ask whom you could be that for in your own place. And ask how much of your sense of who you are depends on being respected or needed.

passages.t: He thought he would die in his nest
passages.happening:
He thought he would die at home in peace, ‘I will die in my nest and multiply my days as the sand’ (verse 18). His roots would spread to the water, the dew would rest on his branches, and his strength would always be renewed.

Men listened to him and waited in silence for his counsel. When he finished, no one added anything. ‘They waited for me as for rain and drank in my words like spring showers’ (verse 23). If he smiled at them, they could hardly believe it. ‘I chose their course and presided as chief. So I dwelt as a king among his troops, as a comforter of the mourners’ (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Job expected a long and peaceful life, and he pictures it in three images: a nest, a tree with deep roots, a bow always renewed.

In a land that depended entirely on seasonal rain, waiting for someone's words as for rain was high praise. The spring showers of March and April, malqosh, were crucial for the last ripening of the grain.

Notice the last phrase of the chapter: Job was a comforter of the mourners. It is the very thing his friends failed to be for him.
passages.asks: Job had been a comforter of mourners, and in his own grief no one comforted him. Ask who comforted you when you needed it, and who did not. And ask who is waiting for that from you now.
